text: Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 9 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the date and time of the assembly shall be agreed by the organiser and the local council of the city, town or village.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate: the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly; the date, starting time and finishing time; the location and the access and return routes; the manner in which the assembly is to take place; the approximate number of participants; the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly; and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 provides that in the event that breaches of the statute or of the law are discovered in the activities of a party or a socio-political organisation, the Ministry of Justice shall warn its leaders in writing, requesting that the breaches be remedied within a fixed time-limit.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 (as originally enacted) provides that the Ministry of Justice shall impose a temporary ban on the activities of a party or socio-political organisation which breaches the provisions of the Constitution or those of the Act, or does not comply with a warning.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: On 21 November 2003, section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 was amended to provide that the Ministry of Justice shall impose a temporary ban on the activities of a party or socio-political organisation which breaches the provisions of the Constitution, and shall inform the party's leadership in writing of the breaches and set a time-limit for remedying them.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that during electoral campaigns the activities of parties and other socio-political organisations may be suspended only by the Supreme Court of Justice.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that during the temporary ban, it shall be forbidden for the party to use the mass media, to disseminate propaganda and publicity, to carry out bank transactions or other operations in respect of its assets and to participate in elections.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that once all the breaches of the law have been remedied, the party shall inform the Ministry of Justice, which shall lift the temporary ban within five days.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that the activities of the party or other socio-political organisation may be suspended for a period of up to six months, and if the breaches of the law are not remedied, for a period of one year.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Article 15(1) of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989 provides that States Parties recognise the rights of the child to freedom of association and to freedom of peaceful assembly.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Article 15(2) of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989 provides that no restrictions may be placed on the exercise of children's rights to freedom of association and peaceful assembly other than those imposed in conformity with the law and which are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security or public safety, public order (ordre public), the protection of public health or morals or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 13(1) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that children shall have the right to membership of non-governmental organisations in accordance with the law.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 13(2) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the State must provide children's non-governmental organisations with financial support, place premises at their disposal and provide them with fiscal incentives.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 13(3) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the involvement of children in politics and their membership of political parties shall be forbidden.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Section 56(g) of the Education Act of 21 July 1995 provides that it shall be the duty of teachers not to involve children in street actions (meetings, demonstrations, picketing, etc.).
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Article 174(1)(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that the organisation and holding of an assembly without prior notification to the Municipal Council or without authorisation from the Council, or in breach of the conditions concerning the conduct of meetings indicated in the authorisation, shall be punishable by a fine imposed on the organisers (leaders) of the assembly in an amount equal to between ten and twenty-five times the minimum monthly wage.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: Article 174(1)(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that active participation in an assembly organised without prior notification or authorisation shall be punishable by a fine of between 180 and 450 Moldovan lei (MDL).
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW

text: On 26 July 2002, a new provision (Article 174(1)(7)) was added to the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985, providing that the involvement of children in unauthorised assemblies shall be punishable by a fine of between 180 and 360 Moldovan lei (MDL).
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL LAW
